# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach temperatures hot enough to vaporize rock on close-orbiting worlds, while the nightside plunges to frigid extremes where atmospheres may freeze out entirely. On the exoplanet WASP-96b... wait, let me reconsider—WASP-96b is not tidally locked in the classic sense.

Better examples include the exoplanet LHS 3844b, where models suggest the dayside reaches 800°C while the nightside remains airless and frozen. Even more relevant are potentially habitable "eyeball planets," where a single ocean lies beneath thin ice on the nightside, centered beneath the star-facing point.

Atmospheric circulation becomes the great equalizer. Winds transport heat from dayside to nightside, and the efficiency of this transport determines whether a tidally locked planet retains a habitable climate. Thick atmospheres like Earth's could moderate temperatures sufficiently, while thin atmospheres fail to prevent atmospheric collapse—where gases freeze onto the nightside surface.
